title: Guidelines
hook: seventh point: do everything with one intention; begin and end the day with it

segments.voice: Yesterday, the commitments of the sixth point. Your line was don't wait in ambush. Did a comeback go unspoken? Day one thousand three hundred three.

Before your feet hit the floor this morning, what was the first thing in your head? A deadline. A phone. Last night's argument. And at the end of the day, what's the last thing? Often it's whatever happened to be on the screen. Both ends of the day get handed to whatever shows up first. The seventh and last point of mind training takes those two moments back on purpose. Its guidelines are short, and one of them is almost too simple to notice: do everything with one intention, and begin and end the day with it.
screen: `THE FIRST THOUGHT OF THE DAY.` → `THE LAST ONE.` → `THE SEVENTH POINT TAKES THEM BACK.`

segments.voice: First, what the guidelines are. The seventh point is a set of short lines for ordinary life, after the cushion. They're not about special practice. They're about the dishes, the inbox, the commute. Second, one intention. A line usually given as: do all activities with one intention. Teachers explain the intention as the wish to wake up for the sake of others, the same wish the whole of mind training has been growing. The idea is a single thread running through everything. Typing an email and sitting in meditation become the same work, done for the same reason. Third, two activities, one at the beginning and one at the end. In the morning, set the intention before the day sets it for you. At night, look back. Teachers describe the evening as a gentle review: be glad for what went well, be honest about what didn't, and set the intention again for tomorrow. No punishment in it, just a clear look and a fresh start. Fourth, steadiness. Another line of point seven is usually given as: whichever of the two occurs, be patient. Commentaries read the two as good fortune and bad. A good day isn't a reason to drop the thread, and a hard day isn't either. The point isn't a perfect day. It's that the thread holds either way. And with that, the seven points are complete: the basics, the main practice, trouble as the path, a whole life's practice, checking yourself, commitments, and now guidelines. Tomorrow the block turns from training the mind to bringing the body down to the floor.
screen: `SHORT LINES FOR ORDINARY LIFE.` · `ONE INTENTION, ONE THREAD.` · `ONE AT THE START, ONE AT THE END.` · `PATIENT, GOOD DAY OR BAD.` · then, large: `ONE INTENTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: begin and end with one intention, starting with a look back. Sit comfortably and let three breaths go by. Run back over the day so far, the way the evening review does. Find one moment you're glad of, and stay with it a breath. Find one that didn't go well, and see it plainly, without scolding. Then put one intention into a few plain words for what's left of the day. Something like: to be of use to someone. Hold it gently while you breathe, and plan to meet it again tonight, just before sleep. The bell holds the time.
Guidelines. The seventh point of mind training: everything done with one intention, set in the morning and renewed at night. Today's word.
Your line: one intention. Today, write your intention somewhere you'll see it tonight, a note on the pillow or the phone, and read it before sleep. Day one thousand three hundred three.

howItsDone: Practitioners of Tibetan mind training often set the wish to benefit others on waking and review the day before sleep, rejoicing in what went well and regretting what did not, then renewing the intention.

look back honestly, glad and sorry, then set it again.

original.note: Sanskrit bodhicitta: the mind set on awakening for the sake of others, the intention mind training keeps returning to.

notes: All slogans paraphrased ('all activities should be done with one intention'; 'two activities: one at the beginning, one at the end'; 'if you can practice even when distracted, you are well trained'). Confirm the sense; translations vary.
The intention identified as bodhicitta, and the evening review as rejoicing, regret and renewal: confirm as a fair summary of traditional commentaries.
The rider-and-horse image is the writer's illustration, not presented as a slogan.
Summary of the seven points in the teach follows the common arrangement (preliminaries; main practice; transforming adversity; a lifetime's practice; evaluation; commitments; guidelines). Confirm.

Editor pass: replaced the 'practice even when distracted' slogan, which belongs to point five and was already used on day 1301, with point seven's 'whichever of the two occurs, be patient' (teach, screen head, match pair); reworked the practice to start from the evening-style review so it doesn't repeat day 1300's set-one-intention sit; softened 'usually' in the hook.
